ImageDescription.value: Den Røde Løber – the red carpet. A sculpture by Marianne Jørgensen at Sydhavnen, the South Harbour mixed-use neighbourhood in Aarhus, Denmark. Photo taken just after construction in August 2025. Official inauguration November 2025. Alt text: Redbrick patterned pathway under a footbridge with buildings and construction work and road and overhead footbridge nearby. Where it meets the main path by the main road, the end is rolled together as if it were a roll of carpet that’s not fully rolled out yet. At one point in the rolled-out section, it bumps up against a footbridge pillar, as if it were imporfectly laid. The effect is both fun and aesthetically pleasing. This is Sydhavnen, the South Harbour mixed-use neighbourhood in development in Aarhus, Denmark. Photo 2025 © Ciara Ní Riain

ObjectName.value: Carpet

Categories.value: CC-Zero|Files with no machine-readable author|Uploaded with pattypan|Safavid carpets|Artworks without Wikidata item|Artworks with known accession number|Images from Cleveland Museum of Art|Art of Iran in the Cleveland Museum of Art|Rugs and carpets in the Cleveland Museum of Art

ImageDescription.value: The Mughals, with their nomadic Central Asian roots, were constantly on the move. They were adept at transporting the trappings of their residences and bases of operation from place to place. Fine carpets and canopies demarcated places of importance, and could be rolled up and moved when the ruler was ready to consolidate his power at a new location. When they settled in stone palaces in India, the interiors were covered with carpets, lending a warmth to the spaces that cannot be felt at the sites today. This carpet is of the type that the Mughals would have acquired for their residences. Mughal paintings are filled with depictions of carpets and textiles, many ornamented, like this one, with delicate and complex palmette-dominated arabesque patterns that evoke a paradisiacal setting.
